demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For an index trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is a poor fit unless the death involved clear interpersonal wrongdoing by a trusted person; nothing else in the profile supports that specific circumstance, so this item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'Need to stay alert' at bedtime implies ongoing external danger, which is less coherent with bereavement-related trauma in the absence of any triggers or appraisals about current interpersonal/physical threat. The rest of the profile centers on loss, self-blame, fragmented reliving memory, and catastrophic interpretations of delay, making this item stand out as mismatched.

vignette:
Amina is a 23-year-old environmental scientist who came to treatment several months after the sudden death of her younger brother, a loss she still struggles to put into words. She is a recent college graduate, single, and living in the United States away from much of her extended African family. At intake, what was most striking was how often she stopped mid-sentence when describing the day he died. She would begin, “I got the call, and then…” and then go quiet, pressing her lips together or shaking her head, as if the rest of the memory had to be pushed back before it could fully form. She was clear that she knew what happened, but said she could not seem to find language for it; when the memory came, it did not feel like a story from the past but like being dropped back into that moment again.

The death had been unexpected. On the day it happened, Amina had been occupied with work and ordinary routines, and she has since become fixed on all the things she did not do. She has come to believe that somebody else would have stopped it, that another sister, another daughter, another kind of person would have known something was wrong sooner, called earlier, insisted harder, done more. In her own mind, the death says something final and condemning about her character. She does not describe this as a passing guilty thought but as a conclusion: that this happened because of the sort of person she is. Alongside that self-attack is a fierce sense of injustice. She returns again and again to how wrong it was that he died so suddenly and that nothing can be undone, no explanation sufficient, no action meaningful enough afterward.

In the weeks after the death, Amina found that time itself had become threatening. If a friend did not text back when expected, if a meeting started late, if a family member’s phone rang unanswered for too long, she was immediately certain something terrible was happening. She did not experience this as worry building gradually. Her body reacted before she had time to think: a jolt in her chest, tightening in her stomach, a rush of alarm that made her reach for her phone or pace the room. Working as an environmental scientist, she spends part of her time waiting on delayed field updates, lab results, and responses from colleagues about site conditions. These ordinary pauses in communication have become loaded for her. A routine delay in a data upload or a late reply from a coworker can abruptly transport her into dread, with her mind racing toward catastrophe before she can tell herself it is only work.

Her nights have become difficult as well. She often lies awake long after going to bed, unable to settle, listening for her phone, checking the time, and dreading the vulnerable, in-between state of sleep. On other nights she falls asleep only to wake again, alert and tense, as though she has been called to respond to something urgent. The exhaustion has sharpened her irritability. Over time, she has noticed herself picking arguments with friends and family, starting drama over minor slights or ambiguous comments. She recognizes that these conflicts pull her into something immediate and familiar; for a little while she can focus on anger, on being wronged in the present, instead of on the death. The cost has been steep. Friends have begun to step back, and conversations with family that might have offered comfort now often turn into accusations, defensiveness, or abrupt silence.

She has also narrowed what she allows herself to see and hear. Television shows, films, or news stories involving sudden deaths, accidents, grief, or families receiving bad news are quickly shut off or avoided altogether. Even the possibility of encountering something similar feels intolerable. At the same time, she ruminates relentlessly, circling the same questions with no relief: what she missed, what she should have done, what kind of person fails in that way. The thoughts do not resolve into understanding; they return as judgment.

By the time she sought help, Amina was frightened by how much of her life had become organized around bracing for disaster and around not letting the memory fully arrive. What finally brought her in was a recent day at work when a delayed call from a field team sent her into such immediate panic that she had to leave her desk and sit in the restroom, shaking, before she even knew what she was reacting to. She said she is afraid that if she lets herself remember everything, she will be swallowed by it, but she is equally afraid of continuing as she is—unable to sleep, alienating people she loves, and living as if every unanswered phone call means another death is already underway. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not to forget her brother, but to be able to think about him without feeling that the worst moment of her life is happening all over again.
